Jamaat must address 1971 issue for its political future
2026-09-19T00:02:27+06:00 | Staff Correspondent
https://www.thedailystar.net/news/politics/news/jamaat-must-address-1971-issue-its-political-future-4276621

Jamaat needs to address unresolved questions surrounding its role in the 1971 Liberation War, an issue former assistant secretary general Abdur Razzaq had repeatedly urged the party to confront, said speakers at a programme yesterday.

Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami must resolve the issue to secure its political future, public acceptance and a place in mainstream politics, they said at a discussion marking the launch of Razzaq’s posthumous memoir at a hotel in Dhaka.

Titled “Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami: Its History and Politics”, the book was published by University Press Limited (UPL).

In the book, Razzaq wrote that repeated efforts to apologise for the party’s role in 1971, drafts prepared over more than two decades, and even an attempt to form a new party had failed because of leadership and internal opposition.

Law Minister Md Asaduzzaman referred to the failed 2016 effort to apologise, saying Razzaq had assessed Jamaat’s role in 1971 and that his statement should be delivered to the nation.

“It [the statement] could have resolved many questions about Jamaat,” he expressed.

He said Jamaat had acknowledged the questions surrounding its role in 1971.

The law minister said Jamaat had sought the removal of its name from the 2026 amendment to the National Freedom Fighters Council Act, which listed the “then Jamaat-e-Islami” among forces that opposed Bangladesh’s independence in its definition of Razakars.

“We replied, ‘We cannot deny the historical truth’.”

He said the word “then” was added after discussions, and Jamaat later did not vote when the amendment bill was passed in parliament.

Asaduzzaman said Razzaq believed Islamic rule should not be imposed from the top. Rather, a state could be shaped by Islamic values if those values developed within society.

The law minister also said he had expected lawyers known to be aligned with Jamaat to attend the event, adding, “Their failure to attend reflects their weakness, narrowness and limitations...”

Razzaq, a senior advocate, was the chief defence counsel at the International Crimes Tribunal until 2013, when he left Dhaka for London. He resigned from Jamaat in 2019 and played a pivotal role in forming the Amar Bangladesh (AB) Party in May 2020 as its chief adviser. He left the party in 2024.

He returned to Dhaka in December 2024 and died in 2025.

Political analyst Prof Dilara Choudhury said all political parties use political manoeuvring, and Jamaat was no exception.

She said the party had sometimes sided with the BNP and at other times with the Awami League. “In this way the party survives.”

She said Jamaat needs major internal reforms to become a mainstream political party amid the country’s changing political landscape.

Speaking virtually, Prof Ali Riaz, vice chairman of National Consensus Commission, urged people not to view the book only through the question of Jamaat’s apology for 1971, saying it should also encourage broader public discussion on Islamist politics.

“I think that if Islamist parties want to do politics, their first task should be to build a democratic state. They must accept popular sovereignty and move forward on that basis. If they can address these issues along with the mistakes of the past, then these discussions may reach a fruitful point.”

The Daily Star Consulting Editor Kamal Ahmed said Razzaq wrote that no party that opposed a country’s independence struggle had ever come to power there and argued that Jamaat must resolve the 1971 issue if it wants to form a government.

He said Razzaq also explained why an apology had failed, noting that a section of Jamaat believed Bangladesh should maintain a special relationship with Pakistan.

A draft apology was discussed in several meetings in 2016 but was rejected at the final stage after the party’s then education secretary warned that Pakistan would be displeased, said Kamal Ahmed.

“...Does that mean the party is still dependent on Pakistan? Will the party move forward by keeping Pakistan pleased? These are important questions.”

Referring to data from the book, he said Jamaat’s permanent membership grew from 650 Rukon in 1958 to 73,045 in 2023, while its number of workers reached 639,000 during the same period.

He said the book puts the party’s associate members at 23 million, while Jamaat received around 23.4 million votes in the recent national election.

He therefore asked, “The simple question is, does the party not get votes from ordinary people?... Does it get votes only from its workers and associate members? Or is the figure for the party’s associate members unreliable?”

Speaking virtually, former senior US diplomat John Danilowicz said the book stood out for its honesty and openness about both the past and the future.

Alongside Abdur Razzaq’s two sons, many of his well-wishers and representatives of civil society attended the event.
